title: Your first program: from one line to two
goal: Produce two lines in order, explain the purpose of the framework and fix one syntax error.

prerequisites.text: In the starting route you have already observed Hello, Nexus! and changed its message. No variables or calculations are needed. If you started here, first open What programming does.

sections.title: A message for the next reader
paragraphs: Previously our display said one sentence. Now make a short note to your future self: what you are studying and how you will proceed. State the intended result in ordinary words first: one line names the subject, another states your approach. We are not calculating yet; we are expressing a clear intention precisely.

The two output statements below execute from top to bottom. Before reading further, predict whether the phrases will be on separate lines. The clue is at the end of each text item. Then compare your prediction with the expected result beside the source.

code.output:
I am learning C++.
One small step.

sections.title: The framework is not a magic spell
paragraphs: A function is a named part of a program that can be called to perform actions. Here we define main. For an ordinary program, main is the entry point after environment setup. The empty () here list no parameters; they belong to the declaration, not to the displayed message. int before main describes the type of its status result.

The braces { and } enclose the body of main. Its statements go inside. return 0; finishes the function with a successful exit status. That status informs the environment and is not part of the visitor message. Later you will meet functions with arguments and calculated results. For now, you need neither new functions nor a different entry-point name.

sections.title: A header and ready-made facilities
paragraphs: The compiler needs declarations for std::cout. #include <iostream> includes the relevant standard header. Think of accessing the description of a ready-made tool, rather than downloading a whole library on every run. The tool-manual analogy is limited: a header is program text processed during the build.

std::cout is the standard output stream in namespace std. It accepts items through <<. One statement can send several items in sequence. For now each statement sends a string literal: text written directly in the source between quotes. Keep iostream, cout, :: and << when changing a message.

sections.title: Source lines and output lines
paragraphs: A new line in the editor makes source easier to read, but does not itself move output to a new line. We explicitly put \n inside both literals. Remove it after C++. and the phrases join: I am learning C++.One small step. The program still compiles, but its result no longer meets our goal.

A semicolon terminates an output statement. Indentation helps a human see the body of main; it does not replace braces or delimiters. Double quotes delimit text. Compare their jobs: quotes belong to a value, ; to a statement, braces to the function body. Knowing the roles makes debugging more deliberate than changing random symbols.

sections.title: Two errors need different help
paragraphs: Remove ; after the first output statement in your own copy, then run. A compilation error prevents the new version from executing. The compiler may point to the next line, where it noticed the problem, so inspect the end of the previous line too. Restore ; and rerun. Do not change the expected output to hide the error.

Now keep valid code but swap the phrases. Compilation and execution succeed, but the result violates the required order. That is a solution error, not a syntax error. The checked result compares specific lines and exit status; it does not prove that you understand the framework. Try explaining without a hint why the return zero was not printed.

sections.title: A new note rather than a copy
paragraphs: Prepare a new class note yourself: Workshop: ready first, then Next: practice. You already know everything required: two statements, two text lines and newlines. Do not add variables, input or conditions. After running, compare the order as well as the words.

Opening the reference solution does not replace your work. If you open help while typing, close it and continue where you left off. In the next lesson, output remains the familiar framework while we explore values of different types.

practice.title: On your own: two lines for class
practice.task: Display Workshop: ready and Next: practice on separate lines in that order. Replace both starter messages and keep the framework. Check the result and explain output versus exit status.

No status zero in the message.
Explain a build error versus an ordering error.
practice.hint: Each output statement needs its own message and \n.

passport.goal: Two lines in the required order.
passport.start: Two placeholder messages in your main.cpp.
passport.knowledge: The first lesson and the framework explained here.
passport.checks: Compare both lines and exit 0. Explain separately.
passport.recovery: Undo the latest edit; view the starter without replacement.

exercises.task: Temporarily remove one ; in your own code. Read the error, restore the symbol and rerun.
exercises.criteria: A build error changes to a successful run; your work is retained.

selfcheck.prompt: The source has two std::cout statements, but the first lacks \n. What happens?
options: The phrases join on one output line
The compiler always reports an error
The phrases automatically appear on separate lines
selfcheck.feedback: A source line break does not specify an output line break.
The header supplies declarations. Statements in main specify output.

selfcheck.prompt: The program printed lines in reverse order and exited with 0. Is the task correct?
options: No: compare order with the task
selfcheck.feedback: Execution success and meeting the task are different.

selfcheck.prompt: What does return 0; do in main?
options: Signals successful termination to the environment
selfcheck.feedback: Output and the function’s status result differ.

selfcheck.prompt: What do {} around the statements of main enclose?
selfcheck.feedback: Quotes delimit a string; these braces enclose the body.

selfcheck.prompt: Explain the header, main, quotes, ; and return 0 in your program.
selfcheck.feedback: Compare your explanation with the walkthrough; it is not graded automatically.
